summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The presence of the O7 antigen in |FRAME: TAX-1392869| strains contributes to the overall virulence of this pathogen, commonly found in extraintestinal infections in humans, and particularly in neonatal meningitis and urinary tract infections., The O7 antigen subunit of |FRAME: TAX-1072458| contains five sugars, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: MANNOSE|, |FRAME: CPD-14794| and |FRAME: L-rhamnose|., Like several other modified sugar nucleotide biosynthetic pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-6942| for an example), the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-14794| starts with |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is activated by |FRAME: TTP| and converted to |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps. These steps are also involved in the synthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| (see |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|) and many other deoxysugars. However, the last two steps of this pathway are catalyzed by unique enzymes - a transaminase (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.33 "EC 2.6.1.33"|) and an acetylase (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.209 "EC 2.3.1.209"|)., The region of the |FRAME: TAX-1072458| chromosome encoding for synthesis of the antigen has been sequenced, and the two functions were assigned to the |FRAME: G-17643| and |FRAME: G-17644| genes, respectively, based on their sequence |CITS: [10517601]|. In a subsequent study both genes were cloned, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| and purified, and their function was verified |CITS: [17905981]|.

pwy_name: superpathway of heme b biosynthesis from glycine
summary: General Background, Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins, including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. , In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in, transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as, |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in, modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|,, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., The protoheme biosynthetic pathway shown here is found in animals, fungi, apicomplexan protozoa, (such as the malaria parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [15144063]|), and members of the, α-proteobacteria. In these organisms the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway starts with glycine, and succinyl-CoA (see |FRAME:PWY-5189|)., In other bacteria (including |FRAME:TAX-562|) and archaea, tetrapyrrole biosynthesis begins with, glutamate instead of glycine (see |FRAME:PWY-5188|). Plants also biosynthesize heme via, glutamate for use in cytochromes and compounds derived from heme. Both the glycine and glutamate pathways are present in the chloroplast-containing |FRAME: TAX-3039| (reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [15576047], [12051904], [16093570]|)., Both tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathways merge at the intermediate |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE|., however, a branch point at |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| leads to biosynthesis of different, compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|),, |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|),, and heme D biosynthesis., A second branch point at |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| leads to biosynthesis of chlorophyll, in plants and bacteriochlorophyll in photosynthetic bacteria (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|)., In eukaryotes, heme biosynthesis spans the mitochondrial (or plastid) and cytosol compartments., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [12177321], [16093570]|. , About This Pathway, This MetaCyc pathway shows many enzymes and genes for heme biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-9606| and the photosynthetic purple nonsulfur α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1063|., |FRAME: TAX-1063| possesses two chromosomes and five additional replicons. Two genes encoding 5-aminolevulinate synthase, hemA and hemT, are present on chromosomes 1 and 2, respectively. Biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole cofactors heme, bacteriochlorophyll, siroheme and cobalamin in this organism is highly regulated and is dependent upon expression of these two isozymes (in |CITS: [7592416], [10491185]|). The hemA gene product is expressed under normal aerobic and photosynthetic conditions, under which the hemT gene product is not expressed. No activity could be demonstrated for the purified, recombinant hemT gene product in vitro |CITS: [10491185]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-1063|, no hemD gene encoding uroporphyrinogen III synthase has been identified. A , gene encoding coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (oxygen-dependent) has been identified as hemF and has amino acid sequence similarities to the eukaryotic enzyme. However, oxygen-independent , (anaerobic) hemN and hemZ encoded forms of the enzyme also exist in this organism, and there is , evidence that these two alleles were duplicated |CITS: [15028685]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1063| and many other , prokaryotes, no gene encoding protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (EC 1.3.3.4) has been definitively identified, , although the gene has been identified as hemG in |FRAME:TAX-562| and hemY , in |FRAME: TAX-1423|. Reviewed in |CITS: [12177321]|. , The ferrochelatase reaction involves incorporation of ferrous iron. In bacteria the mechanisms for acquisition of , ferrous and ferric iron depend upon which form is available in the environment and its abundance. The source , of ferrous iron for this reaction in bacteria may involve direct import by divalent metal ion transporters, more , complex mechanisms involving siderophores, other transport systems, and extracellular reductases |CITS: [12054438]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [12829269]|., In humans, the eight steps of the pathway are divided between the cytosol and the mitochondria, with the final product heme, being synthesized in the mitochondria. The pathway occurs in many cell types and is regulated in a tissue and cell specific manner. The first reaction of the pathway catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-342| or |FRAME: CPLX66-342| is considered the rate-limiting step |CITS: [23471474]|. Defects in any of the enzymes in humans, leads to a group of inherited disorders called porphyrias.

pwy_name: superpathway of heme b biosynthesis from uroporphyrinogen-III
summary: Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. It is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles., It is biosynthesized as protoheme, but different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., This superpathway shows the two routes of synthesis found in the facultative anaerobe |FRAME:TAX-562|. Under aerobic conditions, the transition from |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN| is catalyzed by the oxygen -dependent |FRAME: COPROGENOXI-MONOMER| (EC 1.3.3.3). However, when oxygen is not available, the organism is still able to catalyze this transition, using the readical-SAM enzyme |FRAME: HEMN-MONOMER| (EC 1.3.99.22), which can catalyze the transition without the need for molecular oxygen. This enzyme, which contains an iron-sulfur cluster, is able to break SAM into |FRAME: MET| and a 5'-deoxyadenosineyl radical. This radical can attack |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| and bring about the conversion to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN|., This enzyme is found in many bacteria, but does not appear to be present in archaea or eukarya (the only reference for the enzyme in a eukaryote is in the organism |FRAME: TAX-5911|, but this finding is based on sequence analysis alone, and has not been verified biochemically)., Important branch points within this pathway lead to biosynthesis of other important compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|), |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|), heme D biosynthesis, and bacteriochlorophyll (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|).

|FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| are major components of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage) in animals., They are both |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| polymers composed of repeating disaccharide units,  each containing |FRAME: CPD-12557|  linked by a (1,3) or (1,4) linkage to a uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-12521| or |FRAME: CPD-12515|, with extensive N and O-sulfation. Sulfation occurs to various degrees at position 2 of uronic acid and at positions 4 or 6, or both, of galactosamine. In addition, the amino group of galactosamine is acetylated, Many microorganisms have enzymes that enable them to degrade glycosaminoglycans |CITS: [7654407]|. This ability is particularly important for soil bacteria, which may depend on connective tissues in animal carcasses as a nutrient source., There are several steps in the degradation process. It starts with the cleavage of the polymer into smaller fragments, initially tetra- and hexasaccharides, but ultimately disaccharides. The process continues with the removal of the sulfate groups, and ends with the final degradation of the disaccharides into individual sugars, a step that has not been characterized yet. , The lyases that break the polymer to smaller fragments are classified based on the position of cleavage as either endo-lyases or exo-lyases. The endolytic enzyme can produce products of several sizes, although the final product tends to be disaccharides. The exo-lyases cleave dissaccharide molecules from the non-reducing end of the polymer chain |CITS: [9083041]|. Some lyases, known as chondroitinase AC, can act only on |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A| and |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C| (that contain |FRAME: CPD-12521|), some, known as chondroitinase B, can act only on |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| (that contains |FRAME: CPD-12515|), and some, known as condroitinase ABC, can act on both |CITS: [10618199][9083041]|., The lyases act by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disacchrides. , Chondroitin ABC lyases may help in the regeneration of spinal cord injuries that were thought for a long time to be incurable. Injection of chondroitinase ABC at sites of central nervous system injury, where a glial scar develops, removes the GAG components of ECM chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and attenuates the inhibitory effects to axon growth |CITS: [11948352][11948352][11948332]|., The removal of the sulfate groups is catalyzed by specialized sulfatases that can remove the sulfate groups at either the 4 or 6 positions. The sulfatases have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-585| but the genes that encode them have not been identified |CITS: [5647268]|.

pwy_name: poly(glycerol phosphate) wall teichoic acid biosynthesis // major teichoic acid biosynthesis // glycerol teichoic acid biosynthesis
summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., The best characterized wall teichoic acids are those from |FRAME: TAX-224308| and |FRAME: TAX-655816|, in which the polymeric units are |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY "glycerol phosphate"| and |FRAME: PWY-7815 "ribitol phosphate"|, respectively |CITS: [13684313]|. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 1-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. The anomeric phosphate of the linkage unit is covalently attached to peptidoglycan (PG) via a phosphodiester bond to the C6 hydroxyl of N-acetylmuramate., It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: PWY-7819 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]|. , Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, The main form of wall teichoic acid in |FRAME: TAX-224308 "Bacillus subtilis 168"| (also known as the major teichoic acid of this strain) is a poly-glycerol phosphate polymer. This polymer is composed of about 40 repeating units, and is linked to the peptidoglycan moiety by a linkage unit consisting of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate-N-acetylmannosamine and one to three glycerol phosphate residues |CITS: [2692601]| (the convention used to be that three glycerol phosphate units are present |CITS: [416968]|, but more recent research indicates that it may be only a single unit |CITS: [11882717]|.), , The biosynthetic process can be divided into the following main steps: first, the linkage unit is synthesized, attached to a lipid carrier. Next, the polymeric chain is added, one unit at a time, and is glucosylated. The compound is then transported through the membrane to the outer cell wall, where the glycerol phosphate units are decorated with |FRAME: D-ALANINE|. Finally, the mature molecule is transferred from its lipid carrier to peptidoglycan. A more detailed description follows:, The first step is the attachment of an N-acetyl-glocasamine molecule to the lipid carrier |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P|, by the action of the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35530-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35530|, gene |CITS: [12101296]|. The N-acetyl-glucosamine has to be activated, in the form of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (for more information on the acivation of this donor molecule see the pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|)., Next, an activated |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| unit is added by the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35750-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35750| gene, to generate an N-acetyl-mannosaminyl-β-(1->4)-N-acetyl-glucosamine disaccharide, attached to the lipid., UDP-N-acetyl-mannosamine is synthesized from UDP-N-acetyl-glocasamine by |FRAME: BSU35660-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35660| gene |CITS: [1906927][12107153]|. The last step in the synthesis of the linkage unit is the addition of one glycerol phosphate unit, which is performed by a dedicated |FRAME: BSU35760-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35760|. The glycerol-phosphate unit has to be activated as well, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-606|, which is generated from glycerol-3-phosphate by |FRAME: CPLX-5322|, the product of the |FRAME: BSU35740| gene., Once the linkage unit is ready, |FRAME: BSU35720-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35720|, adds additional glycerol phosphate units successively, until the chain has achieved its final length. A |FRAME: BSU35730-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35730|, adds glucose molecules to the chain, usually attached to the C-2 hydroxyl groups of the glycerol. The glucosylated polymer is then exported (flipped) to the external side of the cytoplasmic membrane by the teichoic acid ABC transporter, which is encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35710| and |FRAME: BSU35700| genes). D-alanine is then added to some of the glycerol units by a machinery encoded by the dlt operon. Finally, the complete teichoic acid is hooked through its linkage unit on the C-6 of a MurNAc residue of a growing peptidoglycan chain in a transfer reaction catalyzed by any of three members of the LCP (LytR-CpsA-Psr) protein family (|FRAME: BSU35840|, |FRAME: BSU35650|, and |FRAME: BSU35520|), releasing the undecaprenyl anchor |CITS:[21964069]|., Most of the enzymes involved in teichoic acid biosynthesis are encoded by the tag genes which are clustered on a 50 kb region of the chromosome |CITS: [1906926]|. The absence of teichoic acid is not lethal for |FRAME: TAX-224308|, and mutations in the |FRAME: BSU35750| or |FRAME: BSU35530| genes, which encode early enzymes in the pathway, result in a morphological change of the cell from rod shape to a sphere shape. However, mutations in late enzymes in the pathway are lethal, due to the accumulation of toxic intermediates.

pwy_name: urea cycle // Krebs ornithine cycle // Krebs-Henseleit cycle
summary: Most organisms have to deal with the excretion of nitrogen waste originating from protein and amino acid catabolism. In aquatic organisms the most common form of nitrogen waste is ammonia (ammonotelism), while land-dwelling organisms developed ways to convert the toxic ammonia to either |FRAME: UREA| (ureotelism) or |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"| (uricotelism). Generally, birds and saurian reptiles excrete |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"|, while the remaining species, including mammals, excrete |FRAME: UREA| |CITS:[13672961][13672962]|. Remarkably, tadpoles excrete ammonia, and shift to urea production during metamorphosis |CITS:[13672962]|., The |FRAME: UREA| is formed in the livers of mammals in a cyclic pathway which was initially named the Krebs-Henseleit cycle after its discoverers, and later became known simply as the urea cycle. This cycle was partially deduced by Krebs and Henseleit in 1932 |CITS: [Krebs32]| and was clarified in the 1940s as the roles of |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE| as intermediates were understood |CITS:[3545062]|., In this cycle, amino groups donated by |FRAME:AMMONIA| and |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| are converted to |FRAME:UREA|, while |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, |FRAME:L-CITRULLINE|, |FRAME:L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE|, and |FRAME:ARG| act as intermediates., Despite the generalization above, the pathway has been documented not only in mammals and amphibians, but in many other organisms as well, including birds |CITS:[4217066]|, invertebrates |CITS:[14465664][5869779]|, insects |CITS: [697760][5791517]|, plants |CITS: [13741005] [13958361]|, yeast |CITS:[11946245]|, fungi |CITS:[4996649]|, and even microorganisms |CITS:[5593971][5709377]|.

General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., About This Pathway, While de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotides starts with |FRAME: UMP| (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|, some organisms utilize this salvage pathway to generate |FRAME: TTP| from |FRAME: CTP|., The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-8624| (dCMP deaminase) (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.12 "EC 3.5.4.12"|). This allosteric enzyme, which is found in Gram-positive bacteria, fungi and metazoa, catalyzes the deamination of |FRAME: DCMP| to form |FRAME: DUMP|, thus providing the nucleotide substrate for |FRAME: HS11096-MONOMER "thymidylate synthase"| (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "EC 2.1.1.45"|)., While another allosteric enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase (EC 1.17.4.1)"| (RNR), plays an essential role in the de novo biosynthesis of all four dNTPs required for DNA synthesis, dCMP deaminase is specifically involved in the production of dTTP. The enzyme is allosterically activated by dCTP and inhibited by dTTP, and is thus regulated by the ratio of dCTP to dTTP in the cell |CITS: [22927644]|. Both dCTP and dTTP appear to bind a single allosteric site located far from the active site, and Mg2+ is involved in their binding |CITS: [7138806]|., The actual reduction of a ribonucleotide to a deoxyribonucleotide (CDP to dCDP in this case) is catalyzed by the rate-limiting |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "EC 1.17.4.1, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|. This enzyme, which plays a central role in DNA replication and repair, can perform the reduction of only the diphosphate form of ribonucleosides., Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase"| (EC 2.1.1.45)., Once |FRAME: TMP| is formed, two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: HS11626-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: CPLX66-1052|.

|FRAME: CPD-10763 Methanopterin| is one of several modified folates that have been identified in Archaea |CITS: [6319137][2624671][1910453][1915350][8501071]| (see also |FRAME: CPD-10764|)., While common in all methanogenic archaea, some C1-oxidizing members of the domain Bacteria also contain an, |FRAME: THMPT|-related carrier, which they use in energy metabolism (see |FRAME: PWY-1723|)., Serving a similar role to the one that folates serve in bacteria and eukaryotes, |FRAME: CPD-10763| carries C1 (single, carbon) fragments between formyl and methyl oxidation levels in methanogens and several other Archaea (see, |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., Despite the similarities, there are clear differences between |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydrofolate) and |FRAME: THMPT|. In the reductive direction, ATP is consumed in the entry of carbon from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into the |FRAME: THF| pathway, but not in entry into the |FRAME: THMPT| pathway., In the oxidative direction, methyl groups are much more readily oxidized on |FRAME: THMPT| than on |FRAME: THF|., Moreover, the redox reactions on |FRAME: THMPT| are coupled to more negative reductants than the pyridine, nucleotides which are used in the |FRAME: THF| pathway |CITS: [10970772]|., The biosynthetic pathway for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10763| was initially elucidated by the use of labeled isotopes, studies and azo dye derivatives |CITS: [8639495]| and has been refined incremently ever since |CITS: [9698382][19746965][21634403][25002541]|. The identification of the enzymes that catalyze the pathway's reactions has proved very difficult, and while all of the enzymes from the early part of the pathway have been identified, most of the enzymes in the later part of the pathway are still unknown., The methyl groups at C-7 and C-9 of the pterin ring of |FRAME: CPD-10763| distinguish it from all other pterin-containing natural products. The methyltransferase that methylates these positions has been one of the enigmatic enzymes of the pathway. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-2190| has been identified, and it has been suggested that in this organism methylation occurs early in the pathway, most likely at the level of |FRAME: AMINO-OH-HYDROXYMETHYL-DIHYDROPTERIDINE| |CITS: [25002541]|. Thus, all compounds in the pathway shown here are dimethylated starting with that intermediate. However, methylation may occur at different steps of the pathway in different organisms. It has been shown that methylation can occur at |FRAME: CPD-16957| in |FRAME: TAX-187420| and |FRAME: TAX-79929| |CITS: [9565696]|.

Please note: to see this pathway properly, please click the "More Detail" button until the compound structures and enzyme names show up., The various folate coenzymes are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis. They also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine (|FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|), and play a role in histidine catabolism |CITS: [11001804]|. , Tetrahydrofolate (tetrahydropteroylmonoglutamate, H4PteGlu1, THF), is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. The folate coenzymes differ in the oxidation state of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions, and the number of glutamic acid moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail (see the pathway, |FRAME: PWY-2161B| for more information on this subject)., There are numerous enzymes that convert the folates from one form to another, and the important ones are included in this pathway., Important folate coenzymes include the mono- and polyglutamylated forms of |FRAME: THF-GLU-N "tetrahydrofolate"| (H4PteGlun), |FRAME: N5-Formyl-THF-Glu-N "N5-formyl tetrahydrofolate"| (5-formyl-H4PteGlun), |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl tetrahydrofolate"| (10-formyl-H4PteGlun), |FRAME: 5-10-METHENYL-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methenyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (5,10-methenyl-H4PteGlun), |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate"| (5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun), and |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (5-methyl-H4PteGlun)., Folate cofactors are particularly important in the methylotrophs - the bacteria that can utilize C1 (single carbon)compounds as their sole carbon and energy source. In the methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-272630|, formaldehyde that enters the cytoplasm condenses with one of the two pterin cofactors, |FRAME: THF-GLU-N "tetrahydrofolate"| or |FRAME:THMPT| (H4MPT), and forms the respective methylene derivative (see the pathway |FRAME: PWY-1722|). , The reaction of formaledehyde with THF is spontaneous |CITS: [5954363][14645276]|, and produces 5,10-methylene-THF, which can be metabolized in two ways: it can enter the serine cycle (see |FRAME: PWY-1622|), where the carbon is used for biosysnthesis, or it may be oxidized via 5,10-methenyl-THF to 10-formyl-THF. 10-formyl-THF can be eventually converted back to THF, releasing formate which is oxidized to CO2 (see |FRAME: PWY-1881|), |CITS: [11889483][10215859][12123819]|. This route is completely reversible, and can flow in both directions; as described above it catalyzes the oxidation of formaldehyde to formate. However, in the other direction, it catalyzes the conversion of formate (which accumulates through the pathway |FRAME: PWY-1723|) to methylene-tetrahydrofolate, which feeds the serine cycle, a formaldehyde assimilation cycle (|FRAME: PWY-1622|)., Vertebrates are not able to synthesize folates, and are completely dependent on folates in their diet. Dietary folates exist mainly as poly and mono-glutamylated 5-methyl-THF and formyl-THF |CITS: [405403]|. Polyglutamyl folates in food are hydrolyzed to folylmonoglutamates by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.9|), and metabolized within the enterocyte into 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1., This monoglutamyl folate is the main form of the vitamin in the plasma |CITS: [13906633][2736319]|, and is transported to peripheral tissues. In the tissues it is demethylated by vitamin B12-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, to monoglutamyl tetrahydrofolate (H4PteGlu1). This H4PteGlu1 form is the preferred substrate of |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.17|, which conjugates glutamate moieties to generate oligo-γ-glutamyl H4PteGlu., The predominant product of this reaction is the hexaglutamyl-HPteGlu form |CITS: [3828323]|., The conversion of 5- methyl-H44PteGlu1 into H44PteGlu1 by vitamin B12- dependent methionine synthase is thus responsible for the conversion of extracellular 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1 from dietary sources into the form that can be used in the biosynthetic pathways |CITS: [3266075]|., In erythrocites folate is largely present in the forms of 5- methyl-H44PteGlun and formyl-H44PteGlun, mostly containing five or six glutamate residues |CITS: [10833329][1247496]|., However, the active forms of folate required for nucleotide synthesis are 10-formyl-H4PteGlun and 5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun., 5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun is also required by |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.53|, in the biosynthesis of methionine. Thus, 5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun is at the branch point of three important pathways |CITS: [3266075]|.

pwy_name: superpathway of sulfide oxidation (phototrophic sulfur bacteria)
summary: General Background, Inorganic reduced sulfur compounds serve as electron donors in many phototrophic and chemotrophic bacteria |CITS: [9328649]|. Sulfide oxidation plays an important role in the global sulfur cycle by reoxidizing the sulfide produced by sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic habitats., Phototrophic purple and green sulfur-oxidizing bacteria use the sulfur compounds as electron donors for reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation during photolithotrophic growth. Light energy is used to transfer electrons from the sulfur compounds to levels found in highly reducing electron carriers such as |FRAME:Ferredoxins| and |FRAME:NADP| |CITS: [2663079]|. Similarly, non-sulfur purple bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1061| and cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-54310| are also able to use sulfide as the electron source for anoxygenic photosynthesis., The purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| carries out the complete eight-electron oxidation of sulfide to sulfate. The process involves the formation of sulfur globules as obligate intermediates |CITS: [9695921]|. Since the initial sulfide oxidation system is periplasmic, the globules are deposited in the periplasm |CITS: [9560425]|. The sulfur in the globules occurs as sulfur chains |CITS: [11782519]| enclosed by a protein envelope |CITS: [7575095]| (see |FRAME: P222-PWY|). , In the process of further oxidation, the sulfur in the globules is reduced inside the bacterial cell to a thiol form, which is transported into the cytoplasm and oxidized by a cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation system. , At this point the cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation pathway is still not completely understood. In addition, there are several oxidation systems, and different organisms employ different systems to achieve this goal. , About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-1049| the initial oxidation of sulfide to sulfur is most likely performed by a periplasmic |FRAME: MONOMER-12314|, which mediates the transfer of electrons from sulfide directly into the quinone pool (this enzyme is described in the pathway |FRAME:P222-PWY|). This process generates the sulfur globules mentioned above. The sulfur in the globules is then reduced again to either |FRAME: CPD-846| or perthiols, which enter the cytoplasm, where they are oxidized to sulfite by the |FRAME:CPLX-7133| |CITS: [9695921]|. While the exact details of the process are still unknown, some of the key players have been identified., According to the latest model, the protein that donates the sulfur substrate to the |FRAME:CPLX-7133| is |FRAME: CPLX-8190 "DsrC protein"|. DsrC carries a sulfur atom on a cystein residue in the form of a perthiol. The source of the sulfur atom is still not clear, but may be DsrL |CITS: [18656485]| or the |FRAME:CPLX-8192 "DsrEFH complex| |CITS: [18952098]|. As the sulfur is transferred to the dissimilatory sulfite reductase an intramolecular disulfide is formed in DsrC, which is subsequently restored to its active form by the |FRAME: MONOMER-16043| subunit of the |FRAME: CPLX-8189| |CITS: [20952577]|., The |FRAME:CPLX-7133| is the enzyme that is responsible for sulfite reduction in sulfate reducing bacteria (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|). However, in sulfur-oxidizing bacteria the enzyme works in the reverse direction |CITS: [18826437]|. Reversed activity of sulfite reductase was first suggested by Peck et al in 1974 |CITS: [4526215]|, and, was investigated in |FRAME: TAX-1049| by Schedel et al, who concluded that the physiological role of the enzyme in this organism is "at all probablity the oxidation of sulfide and/or elemental sulfur to sulfite" |CITS: [Schedel79]|., A later study showed that a sulfite-reductase-defective |FRAME: TAX-1049| mutant, while able to oxidize sulfide to sulfur with specific rates comparable to those of the wild-type, was unable to oxidize the intracellularly stored sulfur, confirming a role of the enzyme in the later stages of the process |CITS: [9695921]|., The sulfite that is formed by |FRAME:CPLX-7133| can be oxidized to sulfate in several routes. The main system in |FRAME: TAX-1049| is the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8835| (see |FRAME: PWY-7457|). An alternative route, which appears to be less important, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8193| and |FRAME: CPLX-8194| |CITS:[trueper82][9004500][11685375]|.

General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathway derives in part from the central metabolic precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from oxaloacetate, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here is similar to pathway |FRAME: PWY-7184| with the exception of the |FRAME: RXN-8850 "flavin-dependent thymidylate synthase reaction"| |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.148 "EC 2.1.1.148"| (catalyzed by ThyX), which substitutes for the more common |FRAME: THYMIDYLATESYN-RXN "thymidylate synthase reaction"| |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "EC 2.1.1.45"| (catalyzed by ThyA). In 2002 it was discovered that some organisms do not posses the thyA gene (named TYMS in animals), and instead have an alternate, novel |FRAME: CPLX-8096| encoded by gene thyX., Both thymidylate synthases catalyze a reductive methylation involving the transfer of the methylene group of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| to the C5-position of |FRAME: DUMP| and a two electron reduction of the methylene group to a methyl group. However, the reductive mechanisms of ThyA and ThyX are distinctly different. The ThyA reductive mechanism uses folate as both a 1-carbon donor and a source of reducing equivalents, producing |FRAME: DUMP| and |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE| as products, and does not involve a flavin coenzyme or a third substrate. In contrast, the ThyX mechanism uses a flavin coenzyme as a source of reducing equivalents, which are derived from NADPH. This NAD(P)H oxidase uses |FRAME: FAD| to mediate hydride transfer in a methylation reaction that results in |FRAME: THF| as a product, rather than the |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE| that is produced by ThyA. The chemical and kinetic mechanisms of ThyX and progress in the design of specific inhibitors are reviewed in |CITS: [19643076]|. Inhibitor design has been specifically addressed in |CITS: [17216455] [18513963]|., Homologs of the thyX gene have been identified in some eubacterial, archaeal, slime mold and viral genomes |CITS: [12029065]|. The genomes of some of these organisms contain only thyX, while others, such as those of |FRAME:TAX-1763| and |FRAME:TAX-1716| species, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765| and |FRAME: TAX-196627| contain both thyA and thyX. The two proteins may function under different phases of the growth cycle (in |CITS: [20636973] [12029065] [12193646] [16707489] [17890305]| and reviewed in |CITS: [12029066] [15046578] [19643076]|)., Because ThyX is found in some important human and animal pathogens, it is of interest as a drug target |CITS: [17216455]|. Some of the bacterial pathogens that appear to posses only ThyX include |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-782|, |FRAME: TAX-139|, |FRAME: TAX-160|, |FRAME: TAX-83558|, |FRAME: TAX-83554| and |FRAME: TAX-813| (in |CITS: [12029065] [12791256]|). Other bacteria that posses only ThyX include |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [17890305]| and the hyperthermophiles |FRAME: TAX-2336| and |FRAME: TAX-63363| |CITS: [15046578]|., Some archaea apparently posses only ThyX and others only ThyA. Those with only ThyX include |FRAME: TAX-56636|, |FRAME: TAX-13773|, |FRAME: TAX-29292|, |FRAME: TAX-2261|, |FRAME: TAX-53953|, |FRAME: TAX-2303|, |FRAME: TAX-50339|, |FRAME: TAX-2287| and |FRAME: TAX-111955| |CITS: [12029065] [15046578]|, and |FRAME: TAX-2242| |CITS: [12423760]|. Conversely, archaea that possess only ThyA include |FRAME: TAX-2234|, |FRAME: TAX-2190|, |FRAME: TAX-2320|, and |FRAME: TAX-145262| |CITS: [15046578]|. It should be noted that many archaea do not contain the substrate tetrahydrofolate as shown in these pathways, and utilize chemically modified tetrahydromethanopterins instead |CITS: [15046578]|., ThyX shows no sequence homology with ThyA and substantially differs from ThyA in crystal structure and reaction mechanism. Evidence has been presented that ThyX is less catalytically efficient than ThyA and it may limit chromosomal replication in bacteria and archaea that posses it |CITS: [18621705]|.

Studies have shown that the capacity to use hydrocarbons as sole carbon and energy source, is very common, and not restricted to any particular group of microorganisms., Examples were found in a wide range of prokaryotic and eukaryotic genera including Gram-negative, and Gram-positive bacteria, yeasts, fungi, and even some achlorophyllous algae |CITS: [7532480]|., One of these organisms is the Gram negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-301|,  isolated from, machine shop cutting oil |CITS: [16560407]|, which can grow on intermediate chain length n-alkanes, (C<sub>6</sub> to C<sub>12</sub>). , This pathway describes the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-148| by this organism., The key enzyme in this pathway is the |FRAME: CPLX-3202|, which is encoded by the OCT plasmid, |CITS: [4515610]|. The |FRAME: CPLX-3202| system introduces molecular oxygen in the terminal carbon, atom of the hydrocarbons at the expense of NADH |CITS: [4403503]| to yield primary alcohols, |CITS: [7592483]|. It is composed of three components - a |FRAME: MONOMER-3842|, a, |FRAME: MONOMER-3844|,  and a |FRAME: MONOMER-1021|., The NADH-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-1021| transfers the electrons from NADH, via the electron, carrier |FRAME: MONOMER-3844|, to the monooxygenase, which reduces the other oxygen atom., The product of the hydroxylase system, |FRAME: OCTANOL|, is then further catabolized by an, |FRAME: MONOMER-1081|, an |FRAME: MONOMER-1082| and an |FRAME: MONOMER-1083|., The final product, |FRAME: CPD-196|, enters the β-oxidation-cycle, and can be utilized, as a carbon and energy source |CITS: [1453953][7532480]|.

General Background, Heptose sugars, mostly glycero-manno-heptoses, are found in the cell surface polymers of many bacteria., They are most common in the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of most Gram-negative bacteria |CITS:[1794130][1618845]|, but are also found in capsules |CITS: [11373120]| and O-antigens |CITS: [10512635]| of some Gram-negatives, and in the S-layer of certain Gram-positive bacteria |CITS:[8720077][10406844][12101286]|. Glycosylation of an autotransporter adhesin protein with glycero-manno-heptose residues has also been reported |CITS: [11442838]|., D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units have been found in different anomeric configurations. The core oligosaccharide of the LPS of |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-573| contain short heptan chains composed of α-configured D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units |CITS: [9346320][9507008]|, while the O-antigen of |FRAME: TAX-703| was shown to contain β-configured residues |CITS: [10712598]|., Prior to their incorporation, the heptose residues are activated by attachment to a nucleotide. Two pathways for the activation of heptose sugars have been described - |FRAME: PWY0-1241| in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and |FRAME: PWY-6478| in |FRAME: TAX-143495|., About This Pathway, The S-layer glycoprotein of the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-143495| DSM 10155 is composed of disaccharide repeating units of |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: CPD-12339| units., The genes responsible for the biosynthesis of the activated form, |FRAME: CPD-12336|, have been identified, cloned, and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified to homogeneity and characterized in vitro |CITS: [11279237]|., The process starts with |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and intermediate of the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|, which is converted to |FRAME: D-ALPHABETA-D-HEPTOSE-7-PHOSPHATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15573| (|FRAME: G-11949|). This compound is converted to |FRAME: CPD-12335| in two steps - the addition of a phosphate group at position 1, and the removal of the phosphate at position 7 (|FRAME: G-11951|, |FRAME: G-11950|, respectively). Finally, the molecule is activated by the addition of GTP, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15576| (|FRAME: G-11952|)., GTP is the only nucleotide that was able to serve as a substrate for this enzyme |CITS: [11279237]|.

Level.2: Amide, amidine, amine, and polyamine degradation
summary: General Background, Creatine is a naturally occurring amino acid that is used to store and supply energy to muscle cells in vertebrates., The name creatine is derived from the Greek kreas (flesh). , The enzyme creatine kinase adds a phosphate to creatine (see |FRAME: CREATINE-KINASE-RXN|), generating, |FRAME: CREATINE-P|. The energy stored in the creatine-phosphate bond can be reused when creatine phosphate, reacts with ADP to regenerate ATP. , In fast-twitch skeletal muscles, a large pool of creatine-phosphate is available for immediate regeneration of ATP, hydrolyzed during short periods of intense work. Because of the high cytosolic creatine kinase activity in these, muscles, the creatine kinase reaction remains in a near-equilibrium state, keeping ADP and ATP almost constant,, and buffering the cytosolic phosphorylation potential that is crucial for proper functioning of cellular ATPases, |CITS: [10893433]|. , Creatine is found in the blood, brain, and muscle of many organisms. , Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate in muscle, and is usually produced at a fairly constant rate, by the body in a nonenzymatic process. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, and is mainly filtered by the kidney and, excreted in the urine. , Both creatine and creatinine can be used by microorganisms as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [Tsuru77]|., At least three different routes by which different microbes degrade creatinine have been discovered, |CITS: [10893433]|., About This Pathway, This pathway for creatinine degradation has been demonstrated in various strains of |FRAME:TAX-507|,|FRAME:TAX-1663|,, Flavobacterium,|FRAME:TAX-1269|,|FRAME:TAX-286|, and |FRAME:TAX-41273| |CITS: [8590669][9734055][Kim86][9563845], [shimizu86]|. This pathway has been studied extensively in |FRAME: TAX-243975| and |FRAME: TAX-68999|. , The first step is the hydrolysis of creatinine back to creatine, which is performed by the enzyme creatininase, (also known as creatinine amidohydrolase). Creatine is hydrolyzed further into sarcosine, releasing urea, by, the enzyme creatinase (also known as creatine amidinohydrolase), and sarcosine is demethylated by either, sarcosine oxidase (EC 1.5.3.1) or sarcosine dehydrogenase (EC 1.5.99.1) to yield glycine and formaldehyde, |CITS: [Tsuru76]|. , A study of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-303| found that all these enzymes were inducible in the presence, of creatinine |CITS: [Tsuru76]|., Since mammals do not have a creatininase function, creatinine is absorberd in the kidneys and released into urine. , As a result, measuring the level of creatinine in the blood and urine provides an accurate measure of renal function., Assays for measuring creatinine concentration are based on biosensors containing the enzymes that, participate in this pathway, meaning that these enzymes are highly important in medical diagnostics |CITS: [10893433]|., Since industrial production is desirable, creatininase and creatinase genes have been cloned, and sequenced from various bacteria, including the creatininase gene from |FRAME:TAX-286| sp. PS-7, |CITS: [7670196]|, the creatinase genes from P. putida DSM2106 |CITS: [3221393]|, |FRAME:TAX-237| sp. U-188, |CITS: [1368564]|, Bacillus sp. B-0618 |CITS: [7474433]|, and the sarcosine oxidase gene of Bacillus, sp. B-0618 |CITS: [7474433]|. , In addition, recombinant enzymes were designed, which are produced constitutively in |FRAME:TAX-562|, |CITS: [1444379][10230521]|.

General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmospheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5265|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the peptidoglycan found in Gram-positive Enterococci , including |FRAME: TAX-1352| and |FRAME: TAX-1354|. The peptidoglycan of these organisms is characterized by having |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of the pentapeptide, and by including a |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| bridge in the crosslinks between glycan strands., Six cytoplasmic steps catalyze the formation of the |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| precursor. This precursor is attached to the memberane acceptor |FRAME:CPD-9646|, generating |FRAME: NAcMur-Peptide-Peptidoglycan|, also known as lipid I., Another transferase adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding lipid II, which carries the full monomer unit, |FRAME:NAcMur-Peptide-NAcGlc-Undecaprenols |., The next step of the pathway describes the amidation of the |FRAME: D-GLT| at the second position of the pentapeptide. , In most of the organisms which have been examined, including |FRAME: TAX-1352|, the α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is present as an amide; i.e. the second amino acid in the peptide sequence is |FRAME: CPD-12296| |CITS: [5219821][6025572][5968582]|. Some characterization of the reaction has been carried out, although the identity of the enzyme that catalyzes it in |FRAME: TAX-1352| is still unknown |CITS: [5638594]|., Following amidation, the final lipid intermediate is transferred by an as yet unknown mechanism through the membrane., The peptidoglycan monomers are polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide crosslinks |CITS: [11320055]|. While some of these enzymes are mono-functional, the main enzymes are bifunctional proteins possessing both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activities |CITS: [9791115]|., Peptide cross-links form between different parts of the peptides depending on the organism. In |FRAME: TAX-1352| the crosslinks includes an interpeptide bridge of a single |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| residue (see |FRAME: PWY-6461|). |FRAME: CPD-302| is added to lipid II by a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15487| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-11868| gene) |CITS: [16510449]| and is subsequently amidated to |FRAME: CPD-3633| by the |FRAME: G-11898|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15525|. summary: General Background, |FRAME: MET| (Met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine (this pathway) |CITS: [3309561]|. Plants use a modification of this pathway, where |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, instead of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting homoserine to cystathionine (see |FRAME: PWY-702|)., Other bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi, can use a different route in which they directly assimilate inorganic sulfur by a sulfhydrylation (see |FRAME:HSERMETANA-PWY|). Level.2: Amide, amidine, amine, and polyamine degradation
summary: General Background, |FRAME:S-ALLANTOIN "(S)-(+)-allantoin"| is a common product of purine degradation. Allantoin is rich in nitrogen, and many organisms are able to degrade and recycle it. Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1458|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, do so under aerobic conditions, while others such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: ORG-5985| and |FRAME: TAX-587| do so only anaerobically., S-Allantoin degradation is not limited to bacteria. Ureide-transporting plants convert fixed nitrogen in their roots to |FRAME:S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|, which are then transported to upper parts of the plant, where they are degraded to release the nitrogen. In addition, some fungi and animals also degrade allantoin., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-64|, comprises the hydrolysis of the internal amide bond of |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN|, forming |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| |CITS: [786256]|. This enzyme turned out to be common to all organisms that can degrade allantoin, and is the first step in all allantoin degradation pathways., |FRAME: ALLANTOATE "Allantoate"| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1091| via one of two routes. In the first route the nitrogen is liberated in a single step in the form of |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: ALLANTOICASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.4"|), while in the other route it is liberated in the form of |FRAME: AMMONIA| in two steps, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD0-2298| (starting with |FRAME: ALLANTOATE-DEIMINASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.9"|)., The next step in the pathway is the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-1091| to |FRAME: GLYOX|. Similarly, this conversion can proceed with the liberation of either |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-LYASE-RXN "EC 4.3.2.3"|) or |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-HYDROLASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.19"|)., Several combinations of these routes have been documented. Some organisms possess pathways that produce solely |FRAME: UREA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5694|), some produce only |FRAME: AMMONIA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5692|), and some produce both (see |FRAME: PWY-5705|). In addition, some anaerobic organisms can degrade allantoin to |FRAME: CPD-389| instead of |FRAME: GLYOX| (see |FRAME: PWY0-41|)., About This Pathway, In this hybrid pathway |FRAME: AT4G20070-MONOMER| and |FRAME: AT4G17050-MONOMER| catalyze the first two steps, producing |FRAME:CPD-1091| and |FRAME:AMMONIA|, while |FRAME: G6275-MONOMER| gives rise to |FRAME:GLYOX| and |FRAME:UREA|. There has been an ongoing debate regarding which pathway(s) operate in plants, but some research suggests that the hybrid pathway may exist in |FRAME: TAX-3847| and |FRAME: TAX-3885| |CITS: [15020640][17594111]|.

pwy_name: NAD salvage pathway III (to nicotinamide riboside) // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide salvage
summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell., Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions., Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these, compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or, NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of , NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while, the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation,, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and, transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases, |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo , pathway, and the salvage pathway., In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from aspartate, (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with tryptophan, (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, This pathway is an NAD salvage pathway which proceeds via the intermediate |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE| (nicotinamide riboside, (N-ribosylnicotinamide, or NR). While the presence of this pathway has been suggested for several organisms, including |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-272131|, |FRAME:TAX-1358|, |FRAME:TAX-727|, |FRAME: TAX-730|, |FRAME: TAX-714|, and |FRAME:TAX-747| |CITS: [12446641]|, it is of particular importance to |FRAME:TAX-727| and other V-factor-dependent members of the |FRAME:TAX-745| family. These organisms lack the enzymes necessary for the de novo synthesis of NAD, as well as most of the enzymes for the more common NAD salvage pathway, and therefore require exogenous NAD supply in the form of one of the V-factor compounds, which include, NADP, NAD, NMN, and NR. However, only the non-phosphorylated V factor, NR, can be transported across the inner, membrane into the cytoplasm, where it can be converted to NAD and NADP |CITS: [12446641]|. Thus this pathway, is critical for these organisms |CITS: [1694467]|. For additional information about V-factor-dependent bacteria, look at the pathway |FRAME: NAD-BIOSYNTHESIS-III|., Since NAD+, which is obtained from extracellular sources, is highly polar, it has to be hydrolyzed before it can be transported across the cytoplasmic membrane for final uptake. A key enzyme in this pathway is the periplasmic NadN protein, encoded by the nadN gene (ushA in |FRAME:TAX-562|). It has been shown that NadN has two activities: firstly, it hydrolyzes NAD+ to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), and secondly, it hydrolyzes NMN to nicotinamide riboside (NR) |CITS: [11395461]|. After NAD+ is transported into the periplasmic space it is hydrolyzed into NMN and AMP by the NAD-nucleotidase activity of NadN. NMN is then hydrolyzed to NR and pyrophosphate, and the nicotinamide riboside thus formed is transported across the inner membrane into the cytoplasm, where it is it is converted back to NMN, and eventually, to NAD+., The identity of the NR transporter has not been confirmed experimentally, but it is suggested that it is encoded by the pnuC gene, although earlier work with the PnuC protein of |FRAME:TAX-28901| serovar Typhimurium suggested that it encodes the transport of NMN |CITS: [6216244][11395461]|., NADP+ is recycled in the same manner, following dephosphorylation to NAD+. In |FRAME: TAX-727|, this dephosphorylation is performed by the outer membrane glycoprotein e (P4), encoded by the hel gene., While the pathway is predicted to be present in |FRAME:TAX-543|, it probably serves a minor role compared to de novo biosynthesis and the main NAD salvage cycle (|FRAME: PYRIDNUCSAL-PWY|). Some of the enzymatic activities associated with this pathway have been described in |FRAME:TAX-543| as early as 1951 |CITS: [14907738]|, but it was only recently that the genes responsible for them were identified. Surprisingly, several activities were found to be functions of the multifunctional protein NadR, which was initially believed to have a role in regulation only |CITS: [10464228][12446641]|.

Toluene is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic compounds can be degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus |FRAME:TAX-286| and closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward bioremediation of environmental pollutants by metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|)., Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various species that involve different initial monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these pathways converge in the formation of 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound is a substrate for ring cleavage enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission pathway, resulting in the formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-3-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-2-OH-PWY|). , The chromosome of |FRAME:TAX-303| F1 contains a gene cluster encoding enzymes that allow this organism to grow on toluene and related compounds as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [2670929], [1916282], [8063106]|. Other strains of P. putida may contain plasmid-encoded genes for toluene degradation (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|). The inducible toluene dioxygenase enzyme hydroxylates toluene to its dihydrodiol derivative by incorporating both atoms of an oxygen molecule into the aromatic nucleus. The dihydroxylated derivative is dehydrogenated to a catechol. Ring fission of the catechol 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) is catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase to produce cis,cis-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate. This compound is hydrolyzed to 2-oxopent-4-enoate, or its tautomeric dienol form cis-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate. This tautomerization occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|. It is not known which tautomeric form is produced by the hydrolase, and which form is used by the hydratase of P. putida F1 in this pathway. However, it has been suggested that the |FRAME:TAX-303| mt-2 hydratase, encoded by the TOL plasmid pWW0, uses the dienol form as a substrate |CITS: [2681159]|, and there is evidence that the |FRAME:TAX-562| hydratase also uses the dienol form as substrate, producing a ketonized intermediate in the reaction mechanism |CITS: [9492273]|. The products of the pathway are pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and acetaldehyde, which may be converted by acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, a central metabolite |CITS: [8063106]|.

General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmpspheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described below., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the peptidoglycan found in several Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1280|. This peptidoglycan is characterized by having |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of the pentapeptide, and by including a pentaglycine bridge in the crosslinks between glycan strands., Six cytoplasmic steps catalyze the formation of the |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| precursor. This precursor is attached to the memberane acceptor |FRAME:CPD-9646|, generating |FRAME: NAcMur-Peptide-Peptidoglycan|, also known as lipid I., Another transferase adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding |FRAME:NAcMur-Peptide-NAcGlc-Undecaprenols "lipid II"|, which carries the full monomer unit., The next step of the pathway describes the amidation of the |FRAME: D-GLT| at the second position of the pentapeptide. , In most of the organisms which have been examined, including |FRAME: TAX-1280|, the α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is present as an amide; i.e. the second amino acid in the peptide sequence is |FRAME: CPD-12296| |CITS: [5219821][6025572][5968582]|. Some characterization of the reaction has been carried out, although the identity of the enzyme that catalyzes it in |FRAME: TAX-1280| is still unknown |CITS: [5638594]|., Following amidation, the final lipid intermediate is transferred by an as yet unknown mechanism through the membrane., The peptidoglycan monomers are polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide crosslinks |CITS: [11320055]|. While some of these enzymes are mono-functional, the main enzymes are bifunctional proteins possessing both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activities |CITS: [9791115]|., Peptide cross-links form between different parts of the peptides depending on the organism. In |FRAME:TAX-1280| the crosslinks includes an interpeptide bridge of five glycine residues. The five glycines are added to lipid II by three enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-11836|, |FRAME: G-11837| and |FRAME: G-11839|, and are donated by charged |FRAME: Charged-GLY-tRNAs| molecules. The crosslinks are formed between the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide and the amino group at the end of the pentaglycine bridge of a second glycan chain., The crosslinking reaction is catalyzed by D-D transpeptidases, a group of enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin-binding proteins"| (PBPs), and involves the cleavage of the D-alanyl-D-alanine bond of the pentapeptides, which provides the energy to drive the reaction. As a result, the peptides in the peptidoglycan polymers are one amino acid shorter than the peptides in the monomers., About the variability of peptidoglycan peptide composition, The peptide moiety, which is bound through its N terminus to the carboxyl group of muramate and contains alternating L and D amino acids, reveals considerable variation among Gram-positive bacteria., The amino acid linked directly to muramate is usually |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, but in some cases, can be replaced by |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: SER| |CITS: [5777324][5965240][4385976][6029599], [5704800][5469569][6033749]|., The most common amino acid in the second position is |FRAME: D-GLT|, but in some cases (in a few, coryneform bacteria) it is hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-48| |CITS: [6072398]|. In some organisms the, α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is modified by amidation or substituted by |FRAME: GLY|, |CITS: [5965232][6064598]|, by |FRAME: GLYCINAMIDE| |CITS: [Interschick70]|, or by |FRAME: CPD0-1578|, |CITS: [4683671]|., The greatest variation occurs at position 3. The residue at this position is usually a diamino acid and is involved in cross-linking through the second amino group. , The most common residue at this position in Gram-positive bacteria is |FRAME: LYS|, as described in this pathway. , The next common residue at this position is |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is present in most Gram-negative bacteria and in some species of bacilli, clostridia, lactobacilli, corynebacteria, propionibacteria, actinomycetales, myxobacteriales, rickettsiae, and cyanobacteria |CITS: [410379][6131881]| (see |FRAME:PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY|)., Other substituitions have been documented, including |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| |CITS:[4884715][14152785][6035494][6031807]|, |FRAME:LL-DIAMINOPIMELATE| |CITS: [14024243][13882624][13525638][11945321]|, |FRAME: CPD-7690| |CITS: [5870104]|, and |FRAME: 5-HYDROXY-L-LYSINE| |CITS: [16562051]|., In some cases the diamino acid in position 3 is not involved in cross linking. In these cases the residue in position 3 can be |FRAME: N-ACETYL-L-24-DIAMINOBUTANOATE|, as in the case of |FRAME:TAX-28447| |CITS: [5704800][5119774]|, or even a monoamino acid, such as |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| |FRAME: GLT| |CITS: [4259817]| or |FRAME: HOMO-SER| |CITS: [5119774][5119774 ][5469569]|., Position 4 and 5 are almost always occupied by two D-alanine residues, which are added as a |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide. In some enterococci and lactobacilli the terminal |FRAME:D-ALANINE| is replaced by |FRAME:D-LACTATE|, |CITS: [1503450]| or |FRAME:D-SERINE| |CITS: [8852545]|, which entails resistance to the glycopeptide antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-12245|., Peptidoglycan is the only cell wall polymer common to both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria,, as well as cyanobacteria.

summary: |FRAME: TAX-83333| is capable of growth on |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE| as the sole carbon and, energy source. |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE| is degraded to |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| in two steps, involving, a |FRAME: AMINEOXID-CPLX| and |FRAME: PHENDEHYD-CPLX|., |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| is then degraded to |FRAME: SUC-COA|, an intermediate of the |FRAME: TCA|., For more information, see |FRAME: PWY0-321|.

|FRAME: PHENYLACETATE Phenylacetate| is a major intermediate in bacterial degradation of many aromatic compounds |CITS: [11260461]|. Microbes can oxidize phenylacetate under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see also |FRAME: PWY-1341|), and the first step in both pathways is the same - the activition of phenylacetate to |FRAME: CPD-207| by a |FRAME: MONOMER-12132 "phenylacetate-CoA ligase"|., Despite the fact that the existence of an aerobic pathway was reported back in 1955 |CITS: [Kunita55]|, the exact chemistry, which is unusual for an aerobic pathway, was solved only in 2010 |CITS: [20660314]|. All of the pathway's intermediates remain in the form of CoA-thioesters, a characteristic typical of anaerobic degradation pathways. , De-aromatization of the ring is achieved by activation of |FRAME: CPD-207| to a |FRAME: CPD0-2362|, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8168|, a multicomponent oxygenase. The reactive non-aromatic epoxide is then isomerized to a seven-member o-heterocyclic enol ether, |FRAME: CPD0-2363|, and the ring is cleaved. The rest of the pathway consists of β-oxidation steps leading to formation of the TCA cycle intermediates |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: SUC-COA| |CITS:[17259607][20660314]|.

summary: Phenylpropanoid compounds are abundant in natural environments, and can originate from putrefaction of proteins in soil or as breakdown products of plants materials such as lignin, various oils, and resins (for the biosynthesis of phenylpropanoid compounds, please see |FRAME: PHENYLPROPANOID-SYN|)., Microbial catabolism of phenylpropanoid compounds plays an important role in the natural degradation of these compounds. In addition, the degradation of several phenylpropanoid compounds is important for industrial applications such as wine making, aging, and storage |CITS: [9143125]|. , This is one of only two aromatic-ring-cleavage pathways found in |FRAME:TAX-562|. That |FRAME:TAX-562| can degrade aromatic acids suggests a wider natural distribution for |FRAME:TAX-562| than the anaerobic environment of the animal gut |CITS: [6345502]|., In the utilization of aromatic acids as a carbon and energy source, |FRAME:TAX-562| employs a branched meta-cleavage pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYPHENYL-PROPIONATE|.  Degradation of these two compounds ultimately yields |FRAME: SUC|, |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|.  Acetaldehyde is further metabolized to yield |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (the second part of this pathway is escribed in |FRAME: PWY-5162|).  , The pathway (including the portion that is described in |FRAME: PWY-5162|) has eight known steps, which makes it among the longest catabolic sequences in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [3531186][8399388][9098055]|., The pathway's enzyme are also able to metabolize |FRAME: CPD-674| and |FRAME: CPD-10797|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6690|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-183 "Gallate"| and structurally related compounds are widely distributed in nature. Plant lignin and tannins are major sources of these compounds, which are degraded by soil microorganisms as part of the terrestrial carbon cycle. , Gallate is also used industrially in inks and paints, and gallate esters are used as food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical antioxidants. Gallate and its derivatives are also of interest in drug development (reviewed in |CITS: [12769668]|. , Gallate and related compounds contain a benzene nucleus and at least 2 phenolic hydroxyl groups. Under aerobic conditions the benzene ring is cleaved by varioius dioxygenases. The benzene nucleus can be cleaved by ortho or meta fission enzymes, leading to different degradation pathways. Several distinct pathways of aerobic aromatic catabolism can be initiated by these dioxygenases, and their distribution among bacteria is complex |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|. Examples of these oxidative pathways are shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|, |FRAME: METHYLGALLATE-DEGRADATION-PWY|, , |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY-2504|., An anaerobic pathway for gallate degradation is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P3-PWY|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME:CPLX-8177 "Gallate dioxygenase"| is a ring-cleavage dioxygenase found in several gallate-degrading organisms that acts specifically on |FRAME: CPD-183| to produce the keto-tautomer of 4-oxalomesaconate |CITS:[16030014][Nogales10]|. The enzyme shares a common ancestor with |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, and has a two-domain architecture that might have evolved from the fusion of the large and small subunits of the latter. In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-285|, it has been shown that |FRAME: CPLX-2701| can catalyze the same reaction, although with lower efficiency |CITS: [5048285]|., The product of the ring cleavage is the keto tautomer of 4-oxalomesaconate, |FRAME: 4-OXALOMESACONATE| |CITS: [Nogales10]|. While it can form the enol form, |FRAME: CPD-185|, spontaneously, it has been shown that in |FRAME: TAX-160488| a dedicated enzyme, |FRAME: G1G01-2697-MONOMER|, catalyzes this conversion |CITS: [Nogales10]|. , The enol form is the substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-2781| |CITS: [11092855]|, and the product of this enzyme, |FRAME: 4-OH-4-ACETYL-2-OXOGLUTARATE|, is cleaved by an aldolase to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, which enter central metabolism |CITS: [12486039]|., Fluorescent pseudomonads, such as |FRAME:TAX-303|, can also cleave gallate by the ortho cleavage enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-2721|, resulting in formation of the lactone |FRAME: CPD-184| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|).

This pathway is required since galactose itself cannot be used for glycolysis directly., In most organisms five enzymes are required to catalyze this conversion: a |FRAME:EC-5.1.3.3|, a |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.6|, a |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.12|, a |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.2|, and a |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.2|., |FRAME:EC-5.1.3.3| participates by producing the galactokinase substrate |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| from its β-anomer |CITS: [8647345]|. The only product of this pathway is |FRAME: GLC-6-P|. The other product, |FRAME: CPD-12575|, is consumed by |FRAME: GALACTURIDYLYLTRANS-CPLX|, forming a cycle., The cycle requires an initial amount of |FRAME: CPD-12575|, which is produced by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.9| |CITS: [COLISALII]|.
