summary: General Background, |FRAME:ALLANTOIN "Allantoin"| is a common product of purine degradation. Allantoin is rich in nitrogen, and many organisms are able to degrade and recycle it., Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1458|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, do so under aerobic conditions, while others such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: ORG-5985| and |FRAME: TAX-587| do so only anaerobically., Allantoin degradation is not limited to bacteria. Ureide-transporting plants convert fixed nitrogen in their, roots to |FRAME:ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|, which are then transported to upper parts, of the plant, where they are degraded to release the nitrogen. In addition, some fungi and animals also, degrade allantoin., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-64|, comprises the hydrolysis of the internal amide bond of |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN|, forming |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| |CITS: [786256]|. This enzyme turned out to be common to all organisms that can degrade allantoin, and is the first step in all allantoin degradation pathways., |FRAME: ALLANTOATE "Allantoate"| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1091| via one of two routes. In the first route the nitrogen is liberated in a single step in the form of |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: ALLANTOICASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.4"|), while in the other route it is liberated in the form of |FRAME: AMMONIA| in two steps, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD0-2298| (starting with |FRAME: ALLANTOATE-DEIMINASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.9"|)., The next step in the pathway is the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-1091| to |FRAME: GLYOX|. Similarly, this conversion can proceed with the liberation of either |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-LYASE-RXN "EC 4.3.2.3"|) or |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-HYDROLASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.19"|)., Several combinations of these routes have been documented. Some organisms possess pathways that produce solely |FRAME: UREA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5694|), some produce only |FRAME: AMMONIA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5692|), and some produce both (see |FRAME: PWY-5705|). In addition, some anaerobic organisms can degrade allantoin to |FRAME: CPD-389| instead of |FRAME: GLYOX| (see |FRAME: PWY0-41|)., About This Pathway, Some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-83333|, are able to utilize allantoin as a sole nitrogen source under anaerobic conditions. , In this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1091| is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-389| by the enzyme |FRAME: G6286-MONOMER|., This enzyme was postulated to be present in |FRAME: ORG-5985| |CITS: [13779743][13924343]|,, |FRAME: ORG-5863| and |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS: [5328936]|, and was eventually purified from, |FRAME: ORG-5863| |CITS: [4399430]|., The |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme has not been purified yet, but its activity was measured in a cell extract, (175 mU/mg) and the gene encoding it mapped |CITS: [10601204]|., |FRAME: CPD-389| is then converted into |FRAME: OXAMATE| and |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| by the, enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-13524|. This activity has been measured in |FRAME: ORG-5985|, |CITS: [14102876]|., It has been suggested that |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| is further metabolized to, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME:AMMONIA| and ATP |CITS: [10601204]|, although an enzyme, that catalyzes the reaction in this direction is yet to be described.

summary: The polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|,, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|) are a group of positively charged organic polycations that are involved in many, biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating, several enzymes |CITS: [3157043][4873311][1409623][2185470]|., While it is clear that polyamines are essential for normal cell growth, we still do not fully, understand their specific molecular functions in vivo |CITS:[3157043]|., |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| are found in all life forms, and, |FRAME:SPERMINE| is found mostly in eukaryotes., In plants, the biosynthesis of polyamines proceeds through |FRAME: CPD-597|., The enzyme involved in reaction from N-carbamoylputrescine to putrescine has recently been described, |CITS: [12435743]|.

Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., |FRAME: MANNITOL| is the most abundant polyol in nature, and is found in bacteria, fungi, algae, lichens and vascular plants., All three naturally-occurring hexitols can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., Each of these hexitols enters the cell via a specific phosphotransferase system, so the first intracellular species is the 6-phospho-derivative |CITS: [1100608]| (note that due to symmetry of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|, their phosphorylation at either end produces the same molecule. When these molecules are phosphorylated at the 6 position by the PTS system, the resulting molecules are named |FRAME: MANNITOL-1P| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, respectively, by conventional nomenclature rules)., In all three cases this sugar alcohol phosphate becomes the substrate for a dehydrogenase that oxidizes its 2-alcohol group to a keto group. In the cases of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: SORBITOL|, the resulting keto sugar phosphate is |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, an intermediate of glycolysis, and hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy |CITS: [6384188][2111176]|., In the case of |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, however, the product of the dehydrogenation is |FRAME: TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE|, which becomes the substrate of a kinase and subsequently an aldolase (in a pair of reactions that parallel those of glycolysis) before it is converted into intermediates (|FRAME: GAP| and, |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|) of glycolysis |CITS: [8955298]|.

pwy_name: 5,8-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate biosynthesis I // futalosine pathway // 1,4-dihydroxy-6-naphthoate biosynthesis I
summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on. Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Much later an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate, which proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-10477|, has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|. Initial analysis of sequenced genomes suggested that the pathway might be present in a variety of organisms |CITS: [19557031]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6262|). Further analysis revealed that the newly discovered pathway may not be identical among all of these organisms. It appears that in some organisms |FRAME: CPD-13324| is converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-10484| (see |FRAME: PWY-7371|), while in others this transformation occurrs via |FRAME: CPD-10477| (as shown in this pathway)., In both pathways |FRAME: CHORISMATE| is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-16467| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-16550| (|FRAME: G-11332|), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-13324| in a complex reaction catalyzed by a radical Ado-Met enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-17947| |CITS: [24083939]|., In the pathway shown here |FRAME: CPD-13324| is deaminated by 6-aminodeoxyfutalosine amidohydrolase (|FRAME: G-17733|) to form |FRAME: CPD-10477|, which is then hydrolyzed by the |FRAME: G-10895| gene product to form |FRAME: CPD-10484|. The later part of the pathway is identical in both pathway variants. The last intermediate shown here is |FRAME: CPD-11420|.

summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). summary: Aerobic bacteria that can utilize |FRAME: ACETYLENE| for growth have been reported several times in the literature, although not often |CITS: [Birch32][37235][DeBont80][Tam83][Germon88][9084145]|. Certain anaerobic bacteria are also able to utilize |FRAME: ACETYLENE| for growth |CITS: [16345714]|. Several strains of strictly anaerobic bacteria that can use  |FRAME: ACETYLENE| as a sole carbon and energy source were purified from marine and freshwater sediments, and were described as a new species in the genus |FRAME:TAX-18| |CITS: [Schink1985]|., In all cases where the pathway has been investigated, |FRAME: ACETALD| was shown to be an intermediate, and |FRAME:ACET| a product |CITS: [DeBont80]|. |FRAME: TAX-29542| converts |FRAME: ACETYLENE| to |FRAME: ACETALD| by a unique tungsten-containing enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-941|. Exposure of this enzyme to oxygen results in conversion of its [4Fe-4S] cluster to a truncated [3Fe-4S] cluster and loss of activity |CITS: [7592321][10447686]|. Other acetylene hydratase enzymes from aerobic organisms have been shown to be molybdenum enzymes that do not cross-react with antibodies raised against the |FRAME: TAX-29542| enzyme, suggesting that acetylene hydratases are a biochemically heterogenous group of enzymes |CITS: [9084145]|., |FRAME: ACETALD Acetaldehyde| is only an intermediate in the pathway, and is subsequently converted to other compounds. In all cases that have been studied |FRAME:ACET| is formed. In the case of |FRAME: TAX-29542|, |FRAME: ACETALD| is also converted to |FRAME:ETOH| |CITS: [Schink1985]|. General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, In several strains, including the respiratory pathogens |FRAME: ORG-6217| |CITS: [19282284]| and |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [11526328]|, and the periodontal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-837| |CITS: [24852504]|, the O antigen contains the modified sugar |FRAME: CPD-14608| [UDP-ManNAc(3NAc)A ]., In the case of |FRAME: TAX-208964| (and other serotype O5 strains of |FRAME:ORG-5927|), the organism possesses two types of O-antigens, which were named the A-band and the B-band. UDP-ManNAc(3NAc)A is only found in the latter |CITS: [8112851]|. In |FRAME: TAX-520| the sugar is part of the A-band trisaccharide |CITS: [11083787]|. |FRAME: TAX-837| also produces two types of O antigens, known as O-LPS and A-LPS, and UDP-ManNAc(3NAc)A is only found in the latter., This modified sugar is synthesized in an activated form as a UDP-linked sugar and is incorporated into the LPS by the action of an inverting glycosyltransferase. It is produced from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| in 5 steps, catalyzed by enzymes whose genes are largely clustered in the genome., In |FRAME: ORG-6217| the cluster was named the B-band O-antigen biosynthesis cluster, and the genes were named |FRAME: G-15292|, |FRAME: G-15293|, |FRAME: G-15294|, |FRAME: G-15295| and |FRAME: G-15296| |CITS:[8939432][12057956]|. In |FRAME: TAX-520| the cluster contains only the last 4 genes (named wlbA, wlbC, wlbB and wlbD, respectively), while genes encoding the dehydrogenase are located elsewhere in the chromosome |CITS: [18621892]|.

summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid, 5,7-diacetamido-3,5,7,9-tetradeoxy-D-glycero-D-galacto-nonulosonic acid) is part of the diverse sialic acid family of α-keto sugars. Members of this family mediate or modulate many cellular interactions in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Many pathogenic organisms can display, bind, or catabolize sialic acids, helping them to evade host immune responses and invade cells (in |CITS: [19282391]|). , Bacteria incorporate sialic acid-like 5,7-diacetamido-3,5,7,9-tetradeoxy-nonulosonate derivatives into virulence-associated cell surface glycoconjugates which may include lipopolysaccharide (LPS), capsular polysaccharide, pili and flagella. These nonulosonate derivatives are unique to microorganisms and may show configurational differences as compared with sialic acid. |FRAME: CPD-13166| is a nonulosonate derivative that shows the same D-glycero-D-galacto absolute configuration as sialic acid (|FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) (in |CITS: [19282391]|). It was first identified in 1994 as a component of |FRAME: TAX-66976| LPS |CITS: [8168511]|. Its correct stereochemistry was determined in 2001 |CITS: [11383892]|. |FRAME: TAX-66976| is the causative agent of Legionnaires' disease., The gastrointestinal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-195| was shown to have novel |FRAME: CPD-13166| derivatives O-linked to serine/threonine residues of flagellin, and genes critical to |FRAME: CPD-13167| biosynthesis were identified |CITS: [17371878]|. In the gastrointestinal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-192222| the complete biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-13167| has been elucidated and was shown to involve genes in the |FRAME: TAX-194| flagellin glycosylation locus |CITS: [19282391]| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, The elucidation of this pathway was based on a combination of bioinformatic, comparative genomic, metabolomic, and functional analyses as discussed in |CITS: [19282391]|. Eleven recombinant enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13167| (CMP-legionaminic acid) the CMP-activated form of |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid) in |FRAME: TAX-192222| were purified and characterized and a biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: CPD-13167| was proposed. The work also provided a method for the large-scale production of |FRAME: CPD-13166| |CITS: [19282391]|. The pathway involves unique GDP-sugar intermediates, rather than the UDP-sugar intermediates found in other pathways (such as pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|), which may provide a means of independent pathway regulation (in |CITS: [19282391]|)., In this pathway PtmF and PtmA were found to efficiently convert |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| to |FRAME: D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P|. The isomerase PtmF was stabilized by copurification with glutaminase PtmA, and together they constituted an unfused D-glucosamine-6-phosphate synthase. The next committed step is catalyzed by a phosphoglucosamine mutase PgmL in a reversible reaction. PtmE is a nucleotidyltransferase with an absolute specificity for |FRAME: GTP| when |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE-1P| is the substrate (this allowed large-scale purification of |FRAME: CPD-13160|). In "one pot" enzymatic reactions, PtmF, PtmA, PgmL and PtmE converted |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| to |FRAME: CPD-13160|. Metabolites were purified and identified by capillary electrophoresis/mass spectrometry analysis and NMR spectroscopy |CITS: [19282391]|., Although still uncertain, the next step was proposed to involve a GlmU catalyzed acetylation of |FRAME: CPD-13160| to |FRAME: CPD-13161|. The enzyme is known to be a bifunctional glucosamine-1-phosphate N-acetyltransferase/UDP-N-acetylglucosamine pyrophosphorylase. The enzyme converted |FRAME: CPD-13160| to |FRAME: CPD-13161|, but not to completion. The authors stated that other candidate enzymes for this reaction are being screened |CITS: [19282391]|., The data and rationale used in elucidating the remaining biosynthetic route to |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid) are detailed in |CITS: [19282391]|. Large scale biosynthesis of this compound could be achieved using two separate "one pot" reactions converting |FRAME: CPD-13161| to |FRAME: CPD-13164|, and this product to |FRAME: CPD-13166|. LegF could efficiently catalyze production of |FRAME: CPD-13167| (CMP-legionaminic acid) |CITS: [19282391]|., The majority of this pathway's enzymes were used in an engineered legionaminate de novo biosynthesis pathway in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [27538580]|.

|FRAME: CPD-10754 "Pseudaminic acid"| is a sialic acid-like sugar that was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [6437679]|. It belongs to a class of nonulosonic acids that are unique to microorganisms and consists of, 5,7-diacetamido-3,5,7,9-tetradeoxy-nonulosonate derivatives that can exhibit configurational differences compared, with |FRAME: CPD-10760| |CITS: [14719362]|., Sugars that belong to this class have been found in many Gram-negative bacterial species as constituents, of important cell surface glycoconjugates, such as LPS |CITS: [14719362]|, capsular polysaccharide |CITS: [11768534]|,, pili |CITS: [11342554]|, and flagella |CITS: [11461915][12791140]|. These modifications are expected to influence, pathogenesis through bacterial adhesion, invasion, and immune evasion |CITS: [16462751]|. |FRAME: CPD-10754 "Pseudaminic acid"| has been reportede only from bacterial pathogens. It is not produced or utilized by humans, nor it is present in commensal bacteria that dominate the human gut microbiome, and this its biosynthesis pathway represents an attractive target for selective inhibition., |FRAME: TAX-210|, which is known as a causative agent of gastric and duodenal ulcers, heavily modifies its flagellin with, |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [12791140]|. Flagellin glycosylation is a necessary modification allowing flagellar assembly, bacterial motility,, colonization, and as a result, virulence |CITS: [12044670][16316188]|., Several genes involved in this process have been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-197| and |FRAME: TAX-210|, and mutations, in these genes completely abolished flagellar assembly and cell motility |CITS: [12044670][12791140][16120604]| ., A six step pathway from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-10754| was ultimately proposed, for |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [16651261]|, and all six enzymes catalyzing it have been identified and characterized, although, not all of them to the same level |CITS:[10954725][16286454][16421095][16651261][16751642]|., When all of the purified enzymes were combined in a single reaction vessel, they were able to catalyze the total, conversion of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-10755|., However, since |FRAME: CPD-10755| apparently inhibits some of the earlier enzymes of the pathway, optimal, conversion was achieved when the process was divided into two reactions, the first one consisting of the first five, enzymes, and the second one consisting of |FRAME: HP0326-MONOMER| alone |CITS: [16751642]|.

This pathway, which operates in cyanobacteria, utilizes a |FRAME: MONOMER-13441| and a |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1240-MONOMER|. In photosynthetic organisms like the cyanobacteria, |FRAME: Reduced-ferredoxins|, which have been reduced by |FRAME: CPLX490-3509| during photosynthesis, is used as the preferred electron donor |CITS: [11289299]|, although |FRAME: Reduced-flavodoxins| can replace ferredoxin when the concentration of the later is low |CITS: [16412515]|.

General Background, Vitamin B12 (also known as adenosylcobalamin or |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|) was discovered in the 1920s after Minot and Murphy reported that they could cure the symptoms of pernicious anaemia by feeding patients with crude liver extract |CITS: [Minot26]| (they received the Nobel prize in 1934 for this discovery)., The unknown factor has been isolated and subsequently crystallized in 1948 |CITS:[Lester48][Rickes48]|, and was given the name vitamin B12 and, as it was shown to contain a cobalt ion, cobalamin |CITS: [12195810]|., Vitamin B12 is one of the most structurally complex small molecules made in Nature. It contains a contracted porphinoid ring with a cobalt ion ligated at its center and further held in place by a lower axial base (a dimethylbenzimidazole) and an upper methyl or adenosyl group. Its biosynthesis is similarly complex, and requires more than thirty genes. It's biosynthesis is confined to only some bacteria and archaea |CITS: [11935176]|., Two main pathways are known for |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthesis - an aerobic pathway (see |FRAME:P381-PWY|) and an anaerobic pathway (this pathway). The main differences between these pathways are the timing of the |FRAME: CO+2| ion insertion and the ring-contraction mechanism (for more about ring contraction, see |CITS: [16592942]|). |FRAME: CO+2| is inserted early on in the anaerobic pathway, and rather late in the aerobic pathway., The two different routes then merge at |FRAME: CPD-689|, and the latter part of the pathway is identical, or at least very similar., About This Pathway, The best characterized anaerobic pathway is the one from |FRAME: TAX-90371|, although much of the early work was performed with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1752| and much of the more recent work was done with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1404|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| starts with the biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole intermediate |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of several important compounds such as |FRAME: Hemes heme| and |FRAME: Chlorophylls chlorophyl|. |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III "Uroporphyrinogen-III"| is converted to a corrin ring by a complex process that involves (among other things) the attachment of eight methyl groups, all derived from |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM)., During the process the ring contracts via bonding of carbons C-1 and C-19, eliminating carbon C-20 from the ring. This contraction process converts the ring from a porphyrin ring to a corrin ring. Both the C-20 carbon and the added C-20 methyl group are lost in the form of |FRAME: ACETALD|., The intermediates formed prior to the formation of the corrin ring are called precorrins. The precorrins are numbered corresponding to the number of methyl groups that have been already introduced. If two different intermediates have the same number of methyl groups, they are also labeled by A or B (as in |FRAME:CPD-675|). If there is still some uncertainty about an intermediate, it is given a temporary designation of X or Y., There is indeed some uncertainty about the path from |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| to |FRAME: CPD-9040|. Early work, performed mostly with |FRAME: TAX-28901|, suggested that this transition may be catalyzed in two steps - the insertion of cobalt into |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-10021|, followed by methylation by |FRAME: G-10057|. However, information gathered from multiple studies, most recently with the aerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1404| that posseses a complete anaerobic pathway, suggests that this conversion may proceed through the oxidized factor intermediates, which is favored for the ease of cobalt insertion. Thus, |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| is first oxidized to |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| by |FRAME: STM3477|. Cobalt in then inserted (either by |FRAME: G-10021| or |FRAME: G-11338|), followed by methylation to |FRAME: COBALT-FACTOR-III| and reduction to |FRAME: CPD-9040| |CITS: [12408752][17567575][16042604][12917443][12686546][23155054]|., The first intermediate with a corrin ring is |FRAME:CPD-9049|. However, this intermediate still needs to be modified extensively. Successive amidation reactions transfer amide groups from two |FRAME: GLN| molecules to the carboxy groups a and c, resulting in |FRAME:CPD-689| - the point where the early-insertion and late-insertion pathways combine. , Additional steps in the pathway of cobalamin biosynthesis are described in |FRAME: PWY-5509| and |FRAME: PWY-5507|.

Methanotrophic bacteria oxidize |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: METOH| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which can be assimilated to form intermediates of the central metabolic pathways. These intermediate compounds are subsequently used for biosynthesis |CITS:[353476][6768606][2110811]|. , There are two known pathways that are used by methanotrophic bacteria for the assimilation of formaldehyde: the serine pathway (this pathway) and the |FRAME: PWY-1861 "RuMP cycle"| |CITS: [8801441]|., In the first reaction of the serine pathway, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which is carried by |FRAME: THF-GLU-N THF| in the form of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate|, is transferred to |FRAME: GLY| to form |FRAME: SER|. The reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1| (SHMT). Two such enzymes, one for assimilation of formaldehyde and one for biosynthesis of glycine from serine, are known in |FRAME: TAX-272630| and |FRAME: TAX-410| |CITS: [241747]|., In the next step |FRAME: SER| is transaminated with |FRAME: GLYOX| as the amino group acceptor by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, to produce |FRAME: OH-PYR| and |FRAME: GLY| (the glycine can be recycled and serve as a substrate for serine hydroxymethyltransferase). |FRAME: OH-PYR Hydroxypyruvate| is reduced to |FRAME: GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.81|, followed by phosphorylation by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.165| to produce |FRAME: 2-PG|., At this point there is a split in the pathway. Some of the |FRAME: 2-PG| is converted by |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.11| to |FRAME: G3P|, which is an intermediate of the central metabolic pathways, and is used for biosynthesis, while the rest of the |FRAME: 2-PG| is converted by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.11| to |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|., |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31|, then catalyzes the fixation of carbon dioxide, conveting |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is reduced to |FRAME: MAL| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37|. |FRAME: CPD-208 "Malyl coenzyme A"| is formed in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.9| and is cleaved by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.24| into |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: GLYOX|., When the last two enzymes (EC 6.2.1.9 and EC 4.1.3.24), as well as EC 1.1.1.81 and EC 2.7.1.165, are found in methylotrophs, they indicate the presence of the serine pathway |CITS: [6768606][1515161][8092853]|., The fate of the |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| depends on wheher the organism possesses the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.1|, which is a key enzyme of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|. If the enzyme is present, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| is converted to glyoxylate by the glyoxylate cycle. However, if the enzyme is missing, as is the case in |FRAME: TAX-272630|, it is converted by the |FRAME: PWY-5741| |CITS: [ 22105076]|. In both cases the resulting |FRAME: GLYOX| can serve as substrate for |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, regenerating glycine and closing the circle., The net balance of this cycle is the fixation of two mols of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and 1 mol of CO<SUB>2</SUB> into 1 mol of |FRAME: G3P|, which is used for biosynthesis, at the expense of 3 mols ATP and the oxidation of 3 mols of NAD(P)H. This does not include the reduction/oxidation of NAD(P)H and/or |FRAME: Etf "electron-transfer flavoprotein"| that occur in the segments of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS| or |FRAME: PWY-5741|., Please note that reaction of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, appears twice in the diagram, (once for the reaction |FRAME: SER| to |FRAME: OH-PYR|, and once for the reaction |FRAME: GLYOX| to |FRAME: GLY|) even though in reality the two reactions are coupled.

summary: General Background, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39|, commonly referred to as ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase or RubisCO, is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both the carboxylation and oxygenation of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| (RuBP). The carboxylation process is generally known as CO2 fixation (see |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|) whereas the oxygenation process is known as photorespiration (this pathway)., The two substrates (CO2 and O2) are competitive with regard to RubisCO, so that an increase in CO2 concentration inhibits oxygenation and vice versa |CITS:[Bowyer97]|. An important factor influencing the rate of oxygenation is temperature, as photorespiration is enhanced by high temperature. The reasons for this are twofold: (i) as temperatures increase the solubility of CO2 diminishes more rapidly than that of O2 and (ii) the specificity factor (Ω) of RubisCO (which represents a measure of the relative specificity for CO2) decreases with increasing temperatures between 7°C and 35°C., While the carboxylation reaction results in two molecules of |FRAME:G3P|, which are processed in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|, the oxygenation reaction forms one molecule of |FRAME:G3P| and one molecule of |FRAME:CPD-67| (2PG). The latter cannot be used in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY| and, instead, is salvaged in the photorespiration pathway. , While photorespiration is essential for the viability of all organisms that perform oxygenic photosynthesis, including cyanobacteria and C3 plants, at ambient CO2 conditions |CITS: [18957552][26994478]|, the photorespiratory cycle results in carbon, nitrogen and energy losses, and, unlike true respiration, does not produce ATP or reducing power. As a matter of fact, despite its name photorespiration does not involve neither light nor respiration., About This Pathway, The main features of the photorespiration pathway include: (i) the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-67| into |FRAME: GLY|; (ii) the processing of two glycines into |FRAME: SER|, CO2 and ammonia; and (iii) the conversion of |FRAME: SER| into |FRAME: G3P|, which is directed towards CO2 fixation via the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|., The first step of the pathway involves the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:CPD-67|, which not only recycles phosphate but also prevents accumulation of this compound, which is a potent inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.1|. The next step is the oxidation of |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| to |FRAME:GLYOX|. In plants |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| is exported to the cytoplasm where it is oxidized in the peroxisomes to |FRAME:GLYOX| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.15|. The |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| generated during this step is detoxified by catalases (see |FRAME:DETOX1-PWY|; |CITS: [15012254]|) in the peroxisome. This step is catalyzed by a different enzyme in chlorophytes and cyanobacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-8363| and |FRAME: PWY-8363|)., Glyoxylate is converted into |FRAME:GLY| by two different enzymes: |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45| and |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.4|. One of the glycine molecues is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, to CO2, ammonia, and a single carbon that is transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate|. The methylene group is then transferred to the second glycine molecule by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, forming |FRAME: SER|. , The serine molecue feeds back into |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, closing a cycle. The main carbon molecule produced by this cycle is |FRAME:OH-PYR|, which is reduced into |FRAME:GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.29|. The pathway ends with the phosphorylation of glycerate to |FRAME:G3P|, which re-enters the Calvin cycle. The phosphorylation is performed by different enzymes in cyanobacteria vs. other photosynthetic organisms., The outcome of photorespiration in photosynthetic cells is loss of carbon via CO2 release, as well as loss of energy, yet the pathway is essential at atmospheric concentrations of CO2. The biological function of photorespiration is not clear. One possibility is that photorespiration is necessary under conditions of high light intensity and low CO2 concentration to dissipate excess ATP and NADPH from the photosynthesis light reactions, and prevent damage to the photosynthetic apparatus |CITS: [11299007]|. Another explanation is that the pathway is necessary for the assimilation of nitrate |CITS: [15272076]|., Engineering tobacco plants by intorducing into the chloroplasts synthetic glycolate metabolic pathways that are thought to be more efficient than the native pathway and blocking glycolate export from the chloroplast resulted in improved photosynthetic quantum yield by 20-40% |CITS: [30606819]|.
